---
title: "Discrete random variables"
execute:
  enabled: true
  echo: true
  warning: false
  message: false
---

The [formal definition of a random variable](defining-random-variables.qmd) requires a measurable mapping from outcomes to values. We now ask a different question: can the possible values be listed one at a time? The answer separates discrete variables from the continuous variables introduced later.

We continue with the [CMUdict pronunciation outcomes](why-random-variables.qmd#the-pronunciation-entry-outcomes). Let $X$ map an entry to its total number of phones.

We separate finite from countably infinite value sets, interpret each value through its preimage event, and then explain why discreteness does not imply that the values lack an order.

```{r}
#| label: load-cmudict-discrete
library(ggplot2)

cmu <- read.csv(
  "data/cmudict/cmudict-pronunciations.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
  check.names = FALSE,
  na.strings = ""
)
cmu$first_phone <- sub(" .*", "", cmu$phones)

stopifnot(
  nrow(cmu) == 133854L,
  all(cmu$phone_count >= 1L),
  !anyNA(cmu[c("phone_count", "first_phone")])
)
```

We declare

$$
\operatorname{cod}(X)=\mathbb Z_{\geq0},
$$

whose values begin

$$
0,1,2,3,\ldots
$$

There is no fixed largest pronunciation length in this declared model, but the codomain values can be placed in a list. This property makes $X$ a [**discrete random variable**](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html).

Recall the three nested ideas. The **codomain** is the value space declared by
the function. The **range** is the set of values the function actually returns
on outcomes in $\Omega$. The [**support**](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html) is the subset of values with positive
probability under the chosen measure. In this finite uniform empirical model,
range and support coincide, but the codomain remains larger.

The [**support**](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html) is the subset that receives positive probability:

$$
\operatorname{supp}(X)
\equiv\{x\in\operatorname{cod}(X):\mathbb{P}(X=x)>0\}.
$$

In the finite empirical distribution over this prepared lexicon, the observed support contains `r length(unique(cmu$phone_count))` values, from `r min(cmu$phone_count)` through `r max(cmu$phone_count)` phones, with gaps allowed. The declared codomain is larger. This distinction prevents an observed maximum from becoming a claim about every possible English pronunciation.

```{r}
#| label: cmudict-discrete-support
phone_counts <- as.data.frame(table(cmu$phone_count))
names(phone_counts) <- c("phone_count", "entries")
phone_counts$phone_count <- as.integer(as.character(phone_counts$phone_count))
observed_support <- phone_counts$phone_count[phone_counts$entries > 0L]

stopifnot(
  sum(phone_counts$entries) == nrow(cmu),
  identical(observed_support, sort(unique(cmu$phone_count)))
)

observed_support
```

```{r}
#| label: plot-cmudict-discrete
#| fig-cap: "The empirical support of total phone count consists of separate integer values."
ggplot(phone_counts, aes(phone_count, entries)) +
  geom_col(fill = "grey65", width = 0.8) +
  labs(x = "Phones in pronunciation", y = "Pronunciation entries") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

## Finite and countably infinite sets

A random variable is discrete when some finite or countably infinite set $\mathcal S$ satisfies $\mathbb{P}(X\in\mathcal S)=1$. <!-- dqr-allow: symbolic-derivation --> *Countably infinite* means that every value can be assigned a position in a sequence even though the sequence has no final value.

The observed phone-count support is finite. The declared nonnegative-integer codomain is countably infinite. Both are discrete because their values occur as separate, listable possibilities.

Support values need not be numerical. The derived `first_phone` variable is a finite, unordered discrete variable: its values are ARPAbet labels. Numerical coding may be convenient in software, but it does not create discreteness.

```{r}
#| label: compare-discrete-types
c(
  distinct_phone_counts = length(unique(cmu$phone_count)),
  distinct_initial_phones = length(unique(cmu$first_phone))
)
```

## Values define separate events

For any observed count $x$, the statement $X=x$ corresponds to the event

$$
\{\omega\in\Omega\mid X(\omega)=x\},
$$

which contains every pronunciation entry with exactly $x$ phones. An upper-tail statement corresponds to

$$
\{\omega\in\Omega\mid X(\omega)\in\{x,x+1,x+2,\ldots\}\}.
$$

For a discrete variable, each support value can be considered separately. A single value may receive positive probability.

## Discrete is not the same as unordered

`first_phone` is usually treated as a set of categories without a numerical distance between them. Total phone count is ordered, and a difference in counts has an interpretation in phones. Both variables are discrete.

Thus discreteness concerns whether the probability-carrying values are separate and listable. It does not determine whether the codomain is ordered or whether arithmetic on its labels is meaningful.

A five-point acceptability score is a useful counterexample to the idea that
numeric display implies continuity. Its values $1,\ldots,5$ are listable and
ordered, but a difference from 1 to 2 need not represent the same response
change as a difference from 4 to 5. The variable is discrete and ordinal.

## Check your understanding

1. Which integer values between the observed minimum and maximum are absent from `observed_support`?
2. Why is `first_phone` discrete even though its values are not numbers?
3. Use `cmu` to define an event containing pronunciations at or above the empirical third quartile of `phone_count`.
4. Explain why the largest observed count does not determine the upper end of the declared codomain.
5. Why is a five-point score discrete even if software stores it in a numeric
   column?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. Between the observed minimum 1 and maximum 32, the absent phone counts are 21–27 and 29–31. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. `first_phone` is discrete because its possible ARPABET labels form a countable set, even though those labels are not numbers. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. The empirical third quartile is 8 phones, so the event $\{\omega:X(\omega)\geq8\}$ contains 35,473 pronunciation entries. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. The largest observed CMUdict phone count only describes this finite resource; the declared codomain can include unobserved larger counts for other pronunciation entries. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
5. The response process permits only five separate values. Storage type does
   not create values between those categories.

</details>

Codomain, range, and support describe different sets, just as discreteness and
ordering describe different properties of a random variable. The [next
page](probability-mass-functions.qmd) assigns mass to each declared value,
including zero mass outside the support.
